newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan commission to probe milk plant closures.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan commission to probe milk plant closures.

text.p: Venezuela's powerful Congressional Finance Commission said Wednesday it would appoint a special group to investigate why Italian dairy giant Parmalat Finanziaria was closing recently privatized milk plants.

Industry sources said the reported closures of up to seven plants throughout the country were a logical, even if tardy, rationalization following Parmalat's $14.7 million high-profile purchase of a 41.4 percent stake in state-owned milk company Indulac in late 1995.

But Finance Commission member Rodrigo Cabezas told reporters, "We're dealing here with national assets that are being decapitalized. The investigation is not going to stop just because it's a private company."
He added that Parmalat officials would be summoned to Congress next Tuesday.

The closures come on the heels of a public relations beating recently meted out on Venezuela's privatization program after national airline Viasa, bought by Spain's Iberia in 1991, went belly up in February.

Exact details of the Parmalat closures that have stirred-up an already disgruntled and flag-waving agricultural sector, are still sketchy. Despite repeated calls, Parmalat officials were unavailable to comment.
But newspaper reports said between four and seven plants would be closed throughout the country, with production absorbed in existing, more modern Venezuelan plants.

Parmalat "is not closing them (the plants) down because they want to, they're old plants. I'm only surprised they haven't done this earlier," said one high-placed industry source who asked not to be identified.
National milk consumption fell an estimated 30 percent last year on a steep recession, forcing milk processors to modernize to maintain margins, the source added.

Venezuela traditionally imports some 40 percent of its milk, but cheap imports ratcheted-up nationalist rhetoric late last year bringing a two-month import ban to western Zulia state, which produces some 70 percent of the nation's milk.
The ban later spread to a headline-grabbing prohibition on cereal imports in central Portugesa state, and scuffles between farmers and police.
"Venezuelan agriculture, like agriculture everywhere, is the last sector to be liberalized," said the source.
"But in the end you either modernize the sector and go through with the pain, or you continue subsidizing it," he added.
Parmalat accounts for some 60 percent of the local powdered milk market, with annual sales of around $200 million, according to industry figures.
